newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown says wants 'stable, competitive pound'. [CORRECTED 00:25 GMT 31/7]
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown says wants 'stable, competitive pound'. [CORRECTED 00:25 GMT 31/7]

text.p: British Finance Minister Gordon Brown reaffirmed his desire for a "stable and competitive pound over the medium term" in an interview published in Thursday's (corrects from Wednesday's) Times newspaper.
Brown said that exporters and industry, hit by the rise in value of sterling, wanted the government above all to pursue consistent economic policies aimed at securing long-term growth.
"I know that what worries exporters and industry most is the instability of stop-go, the return to boom-bust, a repeat of the conditions of the 1980s," he said.

"I am not going to lose sight of the fact that what we want is sustainable long-term growth and that to achieve it we need -- and this is the government's greatest contribution -- a framework for monetary policy that commands confidence," added Brown.

Sterling has continued to soar on foreign exchange markets following Labour's landslide victory in the election in May. The pound has gained around 25 percent in value on a trade-weighted basis over the past year, punishing manufacturers trying to sell overseas.
Several big business lobbies have appealed to the Bank of England, which now sets interest rates independently, not to push up rates further as it could add fresh fuel to sterling's rise.

Pressed on whether he would intervene if the pound maintained its strength, Brown said: "What I am going to do is keep my eye on what matters even more to industry, and that is that we do not return to instability."
Brown said he had no intention of "running after" economic indicators pointing to record credit levels or a slump because of sterling's impact on manufacturing.
"The worst thing that we could do is to follow the indicator of the day and be blown of course," he said.
Brown, who presented his first budget on July 2, said he had no plans for a special autumn budget to attempt to put the brakes on consumer spending.
